Abstract
Organizations and their leaders are recognized as key players in staff well-­being and engagement but there is limited 
longitudinal research with large samples. Moreover, it is not 
clear how specifically leader behaviour impacts on well-­
being. Based on the social identity approach, we argue that 
school leaders who are capable of crafting and clarifying 
what it means to be an organizational member while actively 
representing the groups' interests—an identity leader—will 
be able to foster a positive school climate. In turn, this positive climate should result in a range of positive outcomes 
for school staff members, including better well-­being and 
engagement in their work. Using a longitudinal survey of 
over 6000 school staff, we found support for our hypothesis: school staff members who perceived their school 
leaders as being identity leaders perceived a more positive 
school climate 1 year later, which, in turn, predicted higher 
levels of well-­being (lower burnout, lower stress and higher 
self-­esteem) and engagement in school outcomes (higher 
organizational commitment, team morale and professional 
development). Overall, these results underline the key role 
that school identity leaders play in crafting positive working 
environments and outcomes for staff members.
KEYWORDS
burnout, engagement, identity leadership, leadership, organizational 
climate, school climate, well-­being

The well-­being of staff is paramount to organizational performance and success. This is particularly so 
in educational contexts where poor experiences of school staff directly relate to reduced student performance. For example, emotional exhaustion in school staff is associated with worse students' school 
grades, standardized achievement test scores and school satisfaction (Arens & Morin, 2016). Similarly, 
school staff engagement at work is pivotal. A workforce that is highly engaged will be committed 
towards the goals and mission of schools, showing better performance and team morale (e.g., Bakker 
et al., 2008). Thus, schools that invest in fostering their employees' well-­being and engagement can see 
significant improvements in staff, and subsequently in schools and the quality of education.
One key factor contributing to employee well-­being and engagement is effective leadership 
(Robertson & Flint-­Taylor, 2008). While emerging syntheses demonstrate a consistent association between leadership and employees' well-­being (Kuoppala et al., 2008) and engagement (Decuypere & 
Schaufeli, 2021), most of the work has focused on the dyadic relation between leaders and followers, particularly from a transformational leadership perspective (e.g., Arnold, 2017; Harms et al., 2017; Kuoppala 
et al., 2008). In the current study, we answer the call to go beyond dyadic conceptualizations of leadership (Harms et al., 2017) and approach leadership from a group-­based perspective (identity leadership; 
Epitropaki et al., 2017; Haslam et al., 2020). From this framework, good leadership—and its positive 
influence on followers' well-­being and engagement—is a direct consequence of recognizing and harnessing the power of being a model group member of one's organzation, of being one of ‘us’ and doing 
things for ‘our’ interest (e.g., Steffens, Haslam, Kerschreiter, Schuh, & van Dick, 2014; Steffens, Haslam, 
& Reicher, 2014). However, its potential impact in schools remains untested.
Moreover, while growing evidence suggests that identity leadership promotes better employee outcomes, little is known about how identity leaders can foster these outcomes. Our study examines whether 
school identity leaders can create a positive organizational (or school) climate that promotes better well-­being 
and engagement in staff members using a 3-­year longitudinal design and a broad range of well-­being 
(burnout disengagement, burnout exhaustion, stress and self-­esteem) and engagement measures (organizational commitment, professional development and team morale). Thus, our research is well positioned 
to examine the broad and long-­term consequences of identity leadership along with its mechanism of influence, with direct implications for the way schools and other organizations shape their future leaders.
Leadership and its impact on followers
Leadership and its potential impact on followers' engagement and well-­being has received significant 
empirical attention. Leaders' behaviours—such as their fairness, and support—is associated with staff 
members' well-­being (Dyrbye et al., 2021; Perko et al., 2016; van Dierendonck et al., 2004; Winkler 
et al., 2015) and better performance (student performance; Heck & Hallinger, 2010; team performance; 
Keller, 2006) later in time. In recent years, systematic reviews and meta-­analyses have emerged with 
the goal of integrating what is known about leadership, well-­being and staff engagement. Kuoppala 
et al. (2008) found a positive association between leadership and well-­being (but not engagement) in a 
review of 109 studies. Similarly, in their meta-­analysis on the effect of leadership on staff's mental health 
(including 144 articles), Montano et al. (2017) found a positive association between leadership and their 
followers' mental health. Another meta-­analyses of 157 independent samples by Harms et al. (2017) 
found that transformational leadership and leader-­member exchange (LMX) were associated with less 
burnout and stress, while an abusive style of supervision was associated with these negative outcomes 
(see also Arnold, 2017). In terms of engagement, meta-­analyses have found that transformational leadership is associated with better individual performance (Wang et al., 2011), while LMX leadership is 
associated with more commitment and lower turnover intentions of staff (Gerstner & Day, 1997). In 
contrast, destructive forms of leadership are negatively associated with staff engagement (individual 
performance, commitment and turnover intentions; Schyns & Schilling, 2013).
Importantly, these reviews also highlight several limitations in existing research. First, while much of 
the previous research has focused on transformational and dyadic forms of leadership (e.g., Arnold, 2017),

members (Haslam et al., 2021; Hogg, 2001; Thomas et al., 2013) is quickly gaining interest for its potential 
to improve organizational performance. This group-­form of leadership focuses on leaders as being part of 
a group, as opposed to being apart from the group due to their unique characteristics (being transformational or instructional). Second, the process explaining how group-­based leadership impacts staff requires 
further investigation. Third, the great majority of the previous research is cross-­sectional. In their meta-­
analysis, Montano et al. (2017) conclude that one of the deficiencies in this area of research is ‘a paucity 
of longitudinal studies’ (p. 344; see also Arnold, 2017), and hence it is unclear whether the influence of 
leadership could be observed in time. Our research aims to address each of these limitations.
Identity leadership: A group approach to school leadership
The identity leadership framework was developed to address the group-­based nature of leadership, 
namely that leaders and followers are often part of the same group, and they are subject to group dynamics that influence their relations (Haslam et al., 2021; Hirst et al., 2009; Hogg, 2001). This analysis 
is based on the social identity approach, which recognizes people's capacity to internalize their group 
memberships into their self-­concept, such that the self is defined by ‘we’ and ‘us’ (and not simply ‘I’ 
and ‘me’; Reicher et al., 2005; Tajfel & Turner, 1979; Turner et al., 1987; Turner & Haslam, 2001; Turner 
& Reynolds, 2012). Thinking of ourselves as members of a group directly impacts cognition, emotion and behaviour. A plethora of research has demonstrated that we are more likely to be attracted to 
(Hogg & Hardie, 1991), listen to (Greenaway et al., 2015) and trust (Platow et al., 2012) members of our 
group. There is also evidence that groups are essential to well-­being and have implications for mortality (Steffens, Cruwys, et al., 2016) and mental health (Haslam et al., 2016), including in organizations 
(Steffens et al., 2017). Thus, group processes have important implications for influence and well-­being. 
For example, in schools, staff for whom being a member of school is central to their self-­view (those 
who identify strongly with their school) experience greater job involvement and self-­esteem as well as 
lower depression (Bizumic et al., 2009).
The identity leadership model (Haslam et  al.,  2021; Hogg,  2001; Steffens et  al.,  2018; Steffens, 
Haslam, Kerschreiter, Schuh, & van Dick, 2014; Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, 2014) applied the insights 
gained from the social identity approach to our understanding of leadership. According to this model, 
the most effective leaders will recognize and harness the power of their shared group membership. As 
members of the one group, identity leaders can engage in processes of social influence, and in so doing, 
foster the engagement and well-­being of staff members. Moreover, their shared group membership confers them with the characteristics they need to influence followers, including trustworthiness (Giessner 
& Van Knippenberg, 2008) and charisma (Platow et al., 2006).
In schools—as in organizations more broadly— identity leaders can be characterized by four broad 
behaviours to influence group members (Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, 2014). First, school identity leaders 
would aim at being representatives of their school, embodying the characteristics that define the school 
(i.e., identity prototypicality). Second, school identity leaders would champion the school and its interests 
in ways that are consistent with the school's identity (i.e., identity advancement; Haslam et al., 2021). 
Third, school identity leaders would be entrepreneurs of the school's identity, constructing and clarifying the groups' meaning strategically so that the leaders are concrete manifestations of the group (i.e., 
identity entrepreneurship; Augoustinos & De Garis, 2012). Lastly, school identity leaders would have the 
capacity to embed the group identity by creating environments and structures in which staff members can 
live out the vision of the group (i.e., identity impresarioship; Haslam et al., 2021). In summary, (school) 
identity leaders are prototypical group members (one of ‘us’), champion the group (do things for ‘us’), 
shape a shared group identity (craft a sense of ‘us’), and they embed their vision of the group identity into 
their actions (make ‘us’ matter; Haslam et al., 2021; Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, 2014).
As an emerging—and slowly maturing—area of research, there is increased evidence that identity 
leadership is related to better well-­being and engagement in organizations. A recent meta-­analysis revealed

as more prototypical of the group (Steffens et al., 2021). Participants were also more likely to support a 
political leader when they were perceived as championing the interests of their group (Steffens, Mols, 
et al., 2016; van Knippenberg & van Knippenberg, 2005). Perceived identity entrepreneurship was associated with higher engagement and lower burnout in a repeated measures design (Coffeng et al., 2021). In 
a study of 7294 participants across 28 countries and 31 samples (one of which was longitudinal), higher 
perception of identity leadership was associated with lower burnout (van Dick et al., 2021). In a follow 
up study, identity leadership was associated with greater innovation above and beyond other forms of 
leadership (LMX leadership, transformational leadership and authentic leadership; Bracht et al., 2023). 
However, the application of identity leaders to schools, and its potential longitudinal relations (two or 
more years later), remains to be systematically tested. Thus, the first goal of this research is to test how 
school identity leadership relates to staff well-­being and engagement in a longitudinal model.
Why identity leaders influence followers: Organizational climate
One critical proposition from identity leadership is that leaders impact the everyday experience of 
staff at work. One way of doing so is creating a positive and clear organizational climate, one in which the 
members of the organization feel they belong and thrive. Organizational climate refers to the perceptions of the work environment (Rousseau, 1988), including the meaning attached to the work environment, reward behaviour, policies, practices and procedures (Rousseau, 1988; Schneider et al., 2013). 
These perceptions are shared through interactions with others, becoming meaningful understandings 
of the group/organization (Schneider et al., 2017). A positive organizational climate is associated with 
lower turnover intentions (Ryu et al., 2020), higher staff knowledge-­sharing (Al-­Kurdi et al., 2020) 
and higher organizational commitment (Hu et al., 2022). Organizational climate is also related to better staff well-­being, including lower stress (Loh et al., 2019) and lower burn-­out later in time (Idris 
et al., 2014). In the school context, a positive school climate (shared values and norms, an academic 
emphasis that promotes and supports learning, and positive relations; Thapa et al., 2013) is associated with better well-­being and motivation among staff, including lower burnout rates (Grayson & 
Alvarez, 2008) and higher satisfaction with the job and self-­efficacy (Taylor & Tashakkori, 1995).
In the broad leadership literature, leaders are expected to play an important role in creating and moulding the organizations' socio-­cultural environment. Indeed, there is a dynamic interplay between leaders and 
the social environments they create and promote (Schein, 1992), as was initially demonstrated by Lewin's 
classical studies on leadership styles (Lewin et al., 1999/1939). Since the early 2000s, there has been an increased interest in how and when leaders forge positive climates (e.g., Barling et al., 2002; Cole et al., 2013). 
For example, transformational leadership was associated with better business unit performance partly 
because it was related to a higher achievement culture in the organization (Xenikou & Simosi, 2006). In 
school research, leadership is important for a positive school climate (McCarley et al., 2016) and associated 
school identification (Bizumic et al., 2009). Identity leaders are particularly well suited to support a clear, 
coherent, meaningful and rewarding organizational climate. Given how they champion the group, craft a 
shared meaning and identity, and embed this meaning in everyday practice (Haslam et al., 2021), identity 
leaders can effectively create a work environment (i.e., an organizational climate) that facilitates well-­being 
and engagement. This remains to be tested, especially in a school context.
Current study and hypotheses
The goal of this study was two-­fold. First, it tested whether perceiving school leaders to be identity 
leaders (representatives, crafters, champions and entrepreneurs of the school) impacted on employees' 
self-­reported well-­being and engagement.

temporal association of these relations. Critically, by controlling for initial levels of the mediator

METHOD
Participants and procedure
This research was part of an ongoing collaboration between the Australian National University and 
a government education department in Australia. The project involves staff responses from 89 public 
schools, who answered the survey during the third term of 2018, 2019 and 2020. This is part of their annual school satisfaction survey. Consent was obtained from all respondents. Respondents who changed 
schools in the 3 years of the study (n = 209) were removed from the data given the goal to study the 
influence of the same leadership and organizational climate across years. The number of participants 
that answered at least one of the waves was 6373 (nWave 1 = 3611; nWave 2 = 3606; nWave 3 = 4302). In Wave

Measures
The items of all the measures we employed can be found in Data S1 (https://​osf.​io/​hyrp5/​?​view_​only=​
06865​fd72c​6e464​6839f​a855d​43e8f28). Unless otherwise specified, all items used a Likert scale ranging 
from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree); for each scale, items were averaged such that higher 
scores represent a greater presence of the construct.
Identity leadership
School identity leadership was measured using 15 items of the identity leadership inventory (Steffens, 
Haslam, Reicher, Platow, et al., 2014; Van Dick et al., 2018, 2021), measuring the four components of 
identity leadership (identity prototypicality, identity advancement, identity impresarioship, and identity 
entrepreneurship). An example item is ‘the leadership embodies what this school stands for’. The scale 
had excellent reliability at Wave 1 (α = .98).
Organizational or school climate
The organizational climate of schools—that is, school climate—was measured with the school climate 
subscales of the staff school climate and school identification measurement scale (Lee et al., 2017) at 
Waves 1 and 2. This scale assesses school climate with questions such as ‘staff are friendly to students’. 
The scale had excellent reliability at Wave 1 (α = .96) and Wave 2 (α = .96).
Well-­being
Stress and self-­esteem were measured in Waves 1 and 3, whereas burnout was only assessed in Wave 
3. Stress was assessed with the stress subscale of the short-­form version of the depression anxiety 
stress scale (DASS-­21; Antony et al., 1998). This was adapted to measure stress at work by Bizumic 
et al. (2009; Wave 1: α = .91; Wave 3: α = .91). Participants indicated how much each statement characterized them using a scale from 0 (Does not apply) to 3 (Very much; e.g., ‘I tended to over-­react 
to situations’).
Self-­esteem was measured with a four-­item modified version of the Rosenberg Self-­esteem Scale 
(Bizumic et al., 2009; Rosenberg, 1965). Participants provided their response to items (e.g., ‘I take a 
positive attitude towards myself’) using a 5-­point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 
(Strongly agree). The scale showed good reliability in Wave 1 (α = .80) and Wave 3 (α = .78).
Burnout exhaustion and disengagement were measured in Wave 3 with the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory 
(Halbesleben & Demerouti, 2005; Reis et al., 2015) which includes 16 items, eight measuring exhaustion 
(e.g., ‘There are days when I feel tired before I arrive at work’) and eight focusing on disengagement 
(e.g., ‘Lately, I tend to think less at work and do my job almost mechanically’; Demerouti et al., 2003). 
Both burnout dimensions were reliably measured (αexhaustion = .72; αdisengagement = .80) and answered on a 
4-­point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 4 (Strongly agree).

Engagement in organizational outcomes
Staff's engagement in organizational outcomes was assessed with three outcomes: organizational commitment, professional development and team morale. Organizational commitment was evaluated with a 
shortened version of the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire which assesses how committed 
participants are to the organization and the extent they do their best for their organization (Tetrick & 
Farkas, 1988). Five items (including ‘I talk up this school to my friends as a great organization to work 
for’) were answered. This scale demonstrated good reliability in Wave 1 (α = .80) and Wave 3 (α = .82).
Professional development was assessed with six items created for the purpose of this research. Based on 
education literature, we assessed the extent to which respondents perceived that staff members sought 
and engaged in activities that developed their professional skills, with items such as: ‘Staff are offered 
programs to develop their teaching knowledge and skills’. Staff answered these questions in Wave 1 
(α = .88) and Wave 3 (α = .88).
Team morale was assessed using the morale subscale of the school organizational health questionnaire 
(Hart et al., 2000). Participants responded to items assessing morale in their organization (e.g., ‘Staff 
work with enthusiasm’). This scale showed good reliability in Wave 1 (α = .87) and Wave 3 (α = .86).
Covariates
We included three demographic variables as covariates in our analyses: age, sex and teaching experience, all at Wave 3. Participants reported in what age category they fit (1 = less than 35 years of age; 
2 = 35–49 years of age; 3 = more than 49 years of age) and their sex (1 = Male; 2 = Female; 3 = Other). 
They also reported how many years of experience they had (1 = less than 6 years; 2 = 6–10 years; 
3 = 11–20 years; 4 = more than 20 years). We also controlled for school climate and outcome variables at 
Wave 1, except for burnout which was only measured at Wave 3.
Data analyses
Data used in this study has not been previously used in published articles. Data cleaning, missing data 
analysis, and descriptive statistics were completed using SPSS Version 26 while Mplus 8.3 was used to 
conduct multilevel model path analysis. Mplus analysis codes are available in the Data S1.
To test whether identity leadership at Wave 1 impacted on staff well-­being and commitment to work 
at Wave 3 via school climate (Wave 2), we used a set of hierarchical multilevel models built per dependent 
variable (which were centred at the school level). The multilevel models account for variance of leadership, school climate and outcome variables at both the individual (within) and the school (between) 
level. This within and between variance was examined with ‘null models’ (Model 0) that were run to 
get Muthen's ICCs (intra-­class correlations, akin to the ICC1 but with slightly different estimators; Dyer 
et al., 2005). The ICCs estimate the variance at the between-­level (Goldstein et al., 2002) and determine 
the extent to which the responses within schools are independent from each other (Hox, 2013).
Models then we built hierarchically while also examining the nested nature of the data for paths 
a, b, c and c′ in Figure 1 with random intercepts for all models. This approach was necessary given 
that responses to identity leadership and school climate may also be clustered by (or nested within) 
schools. Following Model 0 (which tested the ‘null model’ to obtain the ICCs for all variables), 
Models 1 tested path c (Figure 1). Specifically, Model 1a examined whether identity leadership at 
Wave 1 predicted the outcome variable at Wave 3 within individuals (i.e., at Level 1), while Model 1b 
tested whether the same pattern occurred at the school level, with school-­averaged identity leadership predicting the outcome variables (i.e., at Level 2). We used Akaike's information criterion (AIC)

RESULTS
Data cleaning and descriptive analyses
Despite efforts to retain all participants across each wave of data collection, missing values analysis 
showed a missing rate across the three waves ranging from 34.6% to 56.4% for identity leadership, 
school climate, burnout (disengagement and exhaustion), stress, self-­esteem, organizational commitment, team morale and professional development. For the demographic covariates (age, gender and 
teaching experience in 2020), the missing rate was between 41.4% and 68%. Little's MCAR test was also 
significant (p < .001) which suggests that the data was not missing completely at random (not MCAR). 
Further exploration of the pattern of missing data suggests that missingness was related to other variables in the dataset (i.e., missing at random [MAR]; Newman, 2014; Tabachnick & Fidell, 2013). To retain 
as many cases as possible and obtain less biased and more powerful estimation of coefficients 
(Newman, 2014), Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML with Estimation Maximization) in 
Mplus was used (Little & Rubin, 2002). FIML is a robust method for managing missing data, comparable to methods such as multiple imputation (Lee & Shi, 2021).2 FIML uses all available data in the estimation process in a single step, including cases with missing values, producing a more efficient model 
and accurate parameter estimates than when missing data is ignored. Table 2 shows the means and

DISCUSSION
The general aim of this research was to advance our understanding of school leadership and its role in 
staff well-­being and engagement. Our specific goals were two-­fold. First, we examined the longitudinal 
impact of identity leadership on well-­being and various types of organizational engagement. This question 
is critical to understand the relations and potential mechanism of group-­based identity leadership, and 
hence, its influence.
In line with H1, staff members who perceived that their school leaders engaged in identity leadership reported less burnout engagement, burnout disengagement and stress, with a marginal association 
for self-­esteem 2 years later while controlling for outcomes at Wave 1 (except for burnout outcomes) 
and demographic variables (teaching experience, age category and gender). These results were found 
at the within-­level. Identity leadership also predicted higher levels of organizational engagement, as 
assessed by organizational commitment, team morale and professional development. This research provides clear evidence that supports the importance of placing the group at the heart of a leaders' ability to 
influence. Effective identity leaders shape both staff improved well-­being and stronger engagement in 
organizational outcomes.
Furthermore, in line with H2, identity leadership was associated with a more positive school climate 
1 year later, and in turn, with better well-­being and engagement the next year. The results at the within-­
level are in line with our hypothesized model (see Figure 1): staff members who believed their leaders 
to be identity leaders at Wave 1 reported a more positive school climate at Wave 2, which was in turn

study is one of few examining the process by which identity leaders impact followers across multiple years.
Our results suggest that individual perceptions of identity leadership predict individual changes of 
well-­being and organizational engagement (i.e., controlling for Wave 1: H1) through changes in school 
climate (i.e., controlling for Wave 1: H2). This was not the case for the between (or school) level. This appears to be the result of adding the outcome variable at Wave 1 at the between-­level as a control variable 
(see Tables S1–S7 in the Data S1 for the models without controls) because overall, there is little change 
across time. It is also possible that the impact of leadership on building shared experiences among staff 
within the whole school may require longer time frames to be detected.
Altogether, this research contributes to a better understanding of identity leadership and its potential 
consequences. Through the leadership's ability to represent, work towards and embed themselves in the 
relevant group, they can directly impact the way organizational staff experience their work environment, including policies, practices and values (Rousseau, 1988; Schneider et al., 2013). In turn, by changing the social environment of the group, identity leaders can support staff well-­being and engagement.
Our results open a potential path forward to reduce burnout and increase organizational engagement, namely by training leaders to become identity leaders. One such approach is the 5R program, 
which is designed to help leaders manage their group identities in the workplace to maximize social influence (Haslam et al., 2017, 2021). In a randomized controlled trial, the program was shown to improve 
leaders' identity-­related abilities (e.g., create a shared sense of ‘us’; maintain team members' identification 
with the group; increase social support), improve team members' intrinsic motivation and confidence 
in their team's abilities, as well as lower burnout (Mertens et al., 2021). The current results suggests that 
identity leadership programs can be a catalyst for a stronger, cohesive group and its potential downstream consequences (well-­being and engagement).
Strengths and limitations
There are several strengths to this research. First, this research is theory-­based, testing a series of psychological processes that had been hypothesized (Haslam et al., 2021) but not tested. Second, this is 
one of few multiyear longitudinal examinations assessing the long-­term associations between identity 
leadership, organizational climate and staff's well-­being as well as engagement. Such investigation has 
not been done, particularly in schools. Additionally, by controlling for the mediator and the outcome 
variables at Wave 1, we were able to assess changes in these processes as a function of identity leadership. 
Third, we had a large sample size (over 6000 participants across 3 years) from 89 different schools. This 
enables us to assess the perspective of staff members across many schools.
However, there are limitations to this research. While all longitudinal research has missing data, 
and even though missing data was treated appropriately and was robust to ways of treating missing 
data (Newman, 2014), a smaller number of missing data would have been preferred. In addition, most 
of the variables were assessed via a survey answered by staff members. Thus, there is a possibility that 
the shared methods bias underly the statistical relationships that are observed. However, the multiyear 
nature of this research provides confidence that these variables are associated beyond the shared nature 
of data collection.
There are also important and fruitful avenues for future research. While our sample size for 
people who changed organizations was insufficient to conduct a meaningful comparison (n = 200), 
future research could examine how new staff who are introduced into schools with high versus low 
identity leadership experience well-­being and engagement. Similarly, future research could investigate the degree to which staff within schools agree that their school has strong versus weak identity 
leadership agreement, and the extent to which such commonality in agreement impacts well-­being 
and engagement.

CONCLUSION
Our research illustrates that school leaders—and in particular school identity leaders—play an important role in shaping and strengthening the organizational climate of schools. By doing so, they are exercising their influence in promoting better well-­being and organizational engagement This is particularly 
important in schools, where there are important flow-­down effects for students and therefore the next 
generation. Identifying ways to promote identity leadership is hence a vital and necessary path forward 
for well-­being and engagement for all.
